artboards.title: 2 · Inside one plan — against a day

annotations.text:
THREE LEVELS, AND NO MORE — 12 Sep

The first draft of screen 1 flattened a goal, three plans and fifteen steps into one list of six. "Build the website" was sitting next to "shape it", and they are not the same size of thing.

  GOAL     Walkbook — the outcome
  PLAN     one deliverable, one owner, one timeline
  STEP     a work item someone finishes

The rule that stops infinite nesting: A STEP NEVER BECOMES A PLAN. If a step is too big to finish, it was never a step — it is a deliverable, and it moves up a level.

All three already exist in the deck: FeatureMeta.goal, FeatureMeta.owner (one field, so "one owner per plan" enforces itself), WorkItem with assignee and due. Nothing new to model — screen 1 just has to draw what is already there.

EVERY PLAN HAS A SPINE — and there are only two

IN ORDER — the app, the site. Step 3 starts when step 2 is done. Dates fall out of the work.

AGAINST A DAY — the launch. Written backwards from 6 October: two weeks out, launch day, a week after. Move the day and every step moves with it, because they are offsets from it, not fixed dates.

That second shape is why "market the app" could never be a step in someone else's ordered plan. It has a different clock.

WorkItem.due already exists and is deliberately in the deck, not the personal store — so these dates land in the calendar and on Today for free.

ONE KIND OF ARROW

Plans wait on plans. Never on a step inside one.

  The site      waits on   The app (its screens)
  The launch    waits on   The site (being live)
  The launch    gives      the words for the page → The site

Step-to-step dependencies across plans would be a project management tool, and you would be back to maintaining a graph. Plan-to-plan is coarse enough to keep in your head and honest enough to block on: launch day will not start if the site is not live.

Inside a plan, order is just order — 1, 2, 3.

IS IT JUST A PROMPT? — no, and this is the part most agent products get wrong

Instructions  (role file, playbook, memory)   → judgement: what good looks like
Tools         (code the agent can call)       → reach: what it can touch
Permissions   (the matrix, per agent per tool) → trust: what it may touch HERE

Only the first is words. A prompt saying "browse the web" with no web tool behind it produces a model that confidently describes browsing it never did.

The registry today: Files, Git, Terminal, Process, Routines, Work, Memory. No web. Browsing arrives as an MCP server installed through Community — built for exactly this: "Machine installs tools for you, Community installs them for your bots", and it reports which agents can actually reach each install.

Open-source design tools come the same way when they speak MCP or have a CLI. Where they have neither, the agent cannot use them, and the honest UI says so.

REVIEW BY DEFAULT (agreed): anything that leaves the machine — push, send, publish, spend — and anything you would call design. Everything else runs and you get the receipt.

TWO DEFAULTS WORTH SETTING NOW

1. Web read is the largest prompt-injection surface an agent has — any page can address it. Fine alone on a marketing agent. Web + terminal + git on ONE agent sits at approval, never full. Screen 4 shows this as a row, not a mode.

2. Permissions follow the work, not the worker. A manager lent to Innotrack runs under Innotrack's grants. That is what makes cross-company employees safe, and it is already the rule in the roadmap.

Shipped templates go. The ToolOffer catalogue stays — the curated list of what a bot may ASK for. Letting an agent find its own capabilities is, in botcatalog.rs's own words, a supply-chain problem wearing a helpful face.

WHAT IS NEW TO BUILD, honestly

1. A proposal — a goal with plans under it, not yet work. Tick at both levels, edit, approve. Approve writes the features AND the playbooks.
2. A plan spine — "in order" or "against a day", and offsets that move when the day moves.
3. Plan-to-plan waits — one arrow, and a plan that will not start when its wait is unmet.
4. Review on a step — fires on done-with-output, not on a tool call. stop_at today fires before a command runs.
5. A manager page — one plan grouped by space, filter chips, reach table, hands.
6. @ reaches any manager — the subtree rule in colleagues() goes.
7. Playbook files at both levels, and the chief of staff offering one across spaces.
8. A web tool — an MCP fetch server through Community, read only.

Example content (Walkbook, the dates, the newsletter) is illustrative. Spaces, managers and agents are this machine's own.
